title: Controlled Operations
summary: Build the controlled-S gate from CNOT and T gates, and identities between gates.
objectives: Build the controlled-S gate from CNOT, T and T† gates
Find the phase a circuit gives to each basis state from the bits and their parity
Rewrite a CNOT with Hadamard gates to swap its control and target
mission: Hardware has no controlled-S gate, so build CS = diag(1, 1, 1, i) using only cx, t and tdg. It multiplies the amplitude of |11⟩ by i and leaves the others unchanged. The circuit must work for any input, including superpositions.
hints: Think of the phase as a sum. Each T adds π/4 for every qubit that is 1. For which pairs of bits (a, b) must the total be π/2, and for which 0?
After qc.cx(0, 1), qubit 1 holds a ⊕ b. A gate on it now acts on the parity. For bits, a + b − (a ⊕ b) = 2ab, so T on each qubit and T† on the parity leave π/2 only when a = b = 1.
qc.t(0), qc.t(1), qc.cx(0, 1), qc.tdg(1), qc.cx(0, 1). The last CNOT puts the parity back into b.

prediction.question: You apply Hadamard gates to both qubits, then a CNOT from qubit 0 to qubit 1, then Hadamard gates to both again, starting from |10⟩ (qubit 1 in 1, qubit 0 in 0). What do you get?
options: |10⟩ unchanged, since qubit 0, the control, is 0
|11⟩, because the whole circuit is a CNOT from qubit 1 to qubit 0
|01⟩, because the circuit swaps the two qubits
prediction.explanation: Conjugating a CNOT with Hadamard gates on both qubits exchanges control and target, so the circuit is CNOT from 1 to 0. Qubit 1 is 1, so qubit 0 flips and |10⟩ becomes |11⟩. A SWAP would need three CNOTs.

challenge.mission: Build the controlled-Hadamard gate with control qubit 0 and target qubit 1, using a single CNOT and single-qubit gates (ry, rz, s, sdg, t, tdg). The built-in qc.ch is not allowed. It applies H to qubit 1 when qubit 0 is 1 and does nothing otherwise. The circuit must work for any input, including superpositions.
hints: A CNOT applies X to the target. Is there a one-qubit gate U with U X U† = H? Then conjugating the target by U turns the X into an H.
X and H both have eigenvalues +1 and −1. A rotation about the Y axis by 45° takes the X axis to the axis (X + Z)/√2 of H.
Apply ry(π/4) to qubit 1, then cx(0, 1), then ry(−π/4) to qubit 1. In circuit order the rightmost factor acts first, so if your result is wrong, test the sign of the angles on the input |11⟩.
